note: Hemophilia B dogs and FIX-knockout mice predicted durable liver-directed AAV-FIX correction; patients lost expression to capsid-specific T cells (Manno 2006), then macaques predicted durability but not the T-cell hepatitis.
label: Hemophilia B (AAV-FIX)

engagement.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony) and FIX-knockout mice, liver-directed AAV2-FIX
engagement.note: Portal-vein AAV2-FIX gave constitutive FIX expression: >17 months in FIX-null mice, ≥8 months in hemophilia B dogs.
engagement.short: Dogs and mice express FIX for months
engagement.quote: Constitutive expression of factor IX was observed, which resulted in the correction of the bleeding disorder over a period of over 17 months in mice.

engagement.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony), portal-vein AAV2-canine FIX
engagement.note: Dogs expressed FIX long-term; patients at 2×10¹² vg/kg lost therapeutic FIX after ~8 weeks as capsid-specific T cells cleared transduced hepatocytes.
engagement.short: Expression lost at 8 weeks, unlike dogs
engagement.quote: duration of expression at therapeutic levels was limited to a period of approximately 8 weeks; (iv) a gradual decline in F.IX was accompanied by a transient asymptomatic elevation of liver transaminases that resolved without treatment.
engagement.confidence: medium (abstract only; Nature Medicine body is paywalled)
engagement.judgement: The abstract itself sets the dog prediction (long-term therapeutic expression after portal-vein rAAV) against the ~8-week human result. AAV2-hFIX16 trial (2001-2004) predates registry results posting; only Spark's long-term follow-up NCT00515710 is registered, with no results.

engagement.model: Nonhuman primates (macaques, scAAV2/8-LP1-hFIXco; 24 animals followed up to 5 years)
engagement.note: scAAV8 programme relied on macaques; six high-dose patients held 5.1% FIX for up to 4 years, stable as in macaques.
engagement.quote: AAV8-mediated factor IX expression remained relatively stable over a period of up to 4 years, in keeping with the stability of transgene expression in animal models, including nonhuman primates.
engagement.judgement: contra to same because the best model changed (AAV2/dog to scAAV8/macaque) and the macaque durability prediction held. Per-dose level did not scale (macaques 1×10¹² vg/kg gave 22%, Nathwani 2007; patients 2×10¹² gave 5.1%) but no primary source states that comparison, so it is not scored. NCT00979238 has no posted results.

dose.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony) and FIX-knockout mice, liver-directed AAV2-FIX
dose.note: Dogs needed ~1/10 the per-kg mouse dose for 1% FIX; by 2002, 1×10¹² vg/kg gave 5-12% in dogs (Mount).
dose.short: Dog dose-response set the human dose
dose.quote: In hemophilic dogs, a dose of rAAV that was approximately 1/10 per body weight that given to mice resulted in 1% of normal canine factor IX levels
dose.confidence: high (verbatim clause, sentence truncated at 27 words)

dose.model: Hemophilia B dogs expressing FIX-Padua (AAV8-canine FIX-R338L, Crudele 2015)
dose.note: FIX-Padua's 8-12× specific activity from dogs held in patients, so 5×10¹¹ vg/kg SPK-9001 gave ~34% FIX without inhibitor or thrombosis.
dose.quote: Furthermore, transgene-derived factor IX–specific activity was consistent with results from preclinical studies.
dose.reason: Padua activity gain held in patients
dose.judgement: Manno 2006 (dogs 1×10¹² vg/kg gave 5-12%; patients 2×10¹² gave a therapeutic peak) is a within-2× dose match in substance, but the abstract never states the dose comparison and the body is paywalled, so it is not scored. The later product-level NHP-to-patient match (Spronck 2019 predicted 'upper mild into the non-hemophilic' FIX at 2×10¹³ gc/kg; HOPE-B +34 percentage points at 18 months, Pipe 2023, NCT03569891 results posted 2022-10-10) leaves the status unchanged; FDA's Hemgenix review summarises the NHP data without comparing. Registry date is NCT02484092.

efficacy.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony), intramuscular AAV2-canine FIX
efficacy.note: First AAV-FIX use in hemophilia B dogs: dose-dependent, stable partial correction of clotting times for >17 months.
efficacy.quote: The five hemophilia B dogs treated showed stable, vector dose-dependent partial correction of the whole blood clotting time and, at higher doses, of the activated partial thromboplastin time.

efficacy.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony), portal-vein AAV2-canine FIX
efficacy.note: Dogs showed sustained phenotypic correction (>17 months); the high-dose patient's therapeutic FIX, and any protection, lasted about 8 weeks.
efficacy.short: Correction transient, not sustained as in dogs
efficacy.quote: duration of expression at therapeutic levels was limited to a period of approximately 8 weeks
efficacy.confidence: medium (abstract only; Nature Medicine body is paywalled); bleeding outcomes not reported, therapeutic FIX level is the efficacy surrogate
efficacy.judgement: Dog prediction quoted in the same abstract: 'a single portal vein infusion of a recombinant adeno-associated viral vector (rAAV) expressing canine Factor IX (F.IX) resulted in long-term expression of therapeutic levels of F.IX in dogs with severe hemophilia B.' AAV2-hFIX16 trial (2001-2004) predates registry results posting; only Spark's long-term follow-up NCT00515710 is registered, with no results.

efficacy.model: Nonhuman primates (macaques, scAAV2/8-LP1-hFIXco; 24 animals followed up to 5 years)
efficacy.note: Durable 5% FIX cut bleeding >90% and stopped prophylaxis in most high-dose patients, for 4 years, as macaques predicted.
efficacy.quote: AAV8-mediated factor IX expression remained relatively stable over a period of up to 4 years, in keeping with the stability of transgene expression in animal models, including nonhuman primates.
efficacy.judgement: Same quote as engagement: the source ties durability to the macaque data and reports the bleeding benefit separately. George 2017 later put dog and patient durability side by side ('4 years in a clinical trial and for 8 years in canine hemophilia B models'); same status, so no new entry.

safety.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony) and FIX-knockout mice, liver-directed AAV2-FIX
safety.note: Neither dogs nor mice showed toxicity after portal-vein AAV2-FIX; no capsid T-cell response was looked for or seen.
safety.short: No toxicity in dogs or mice
safety.quote: There was no associated toxicity with infusion in either animal model.

safety.model: Hemophilia B dogs (Chapel Hill colony) and FIX-knockout mice, liver-directed AAV2-FIX
safety.note: Patients developed transient transaminitis as capsid-specific T cells destroyed transduced hepatocytes, a toxicity no dog or mouse had shown.
safety.short: Capsid T-cell hepatitis unseen in animals
safety.quote: Further studies suggested that destruction of transduced hepatocytes by cell-mediated immunity targeting antigens of the AAV capsid caused both the decline in F.IX and the transient transaminitis.
safety.confidence: medium (abstract only; Nature Medicine body is paywalled); the explicit 'not observed in animal models' sentence is in Nathwani 2014 (next entry)
safety.judgement: comparison_stated false: the abstract reports the human toxicity and the dogs' long-term expression but does not put animal safety beside it; juxtaposed with Snyder 1999 ('no associated toxicity ... in either animal model'). AAV2-hFIX16 trial (2001-2004) predates registry results posting; only Spark's long-term follow-up NCT00515710 is registered, with no results.

safety.model: Nonhuman primates (24 macaques, scAAV2/8-LP1-hFIXco: no capsid-specific CTL, no toxicity)
safety.note: Both initial high-dose patients had ALT rises from capsid-directed T cells; 24 macaques followed up to 5 years had shown none.
safety.quote: This complication had not been observed in animal models.
safety.reason: Capsid T-cell hepatitis absent in animals
safety.judgement: Second contra entry because the best model changed to macaques (Nathwani 2011 Mol Ther: no capsid-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes, no toxicity) and was contradicted again; steroid-managed ALT rises recur with every later product (George 2017, HOPE-B).
